Diagnostics

Justin Chase

19 October 2026

Source: vignettes/diagnostics.Rmd
diagnostics.Rmd

This article needs two optional packages: gstat, which fits the variogram behind the autocorrelation range, and ggplot2 for the figures. When either is missing the code is shown but not run, and a note at the top says so.

Four questions a score does not answer

A cross-validated RMSE tells you how far the predictions fell from the held-out values. It is silent on four things that decide whether the analysis holds up: whether the model left spatial structure in its residuals, whether the standard errors on aggregated values are the width they claim, whether a cell mean is the best estimate of that cell available, and where on the map the score applies at all. A fifth section shows two ways the score itself can be wrong, and a sixth reads the warnings summarize_by_cell() raises about pooled cell values.

A fixture and a model that is wrong in a known way

The response is driven by one real predictor and by a spatial field the model never sees. b is noise. A linear model on a and b therefore leaves the field in its residuals, which is what the first diagnostic should detect.

library(sf)
library(spatialkit)

set.seed(11)
n  <- 350
xy <- data.frame(x = 5e5 + runif(n, 0, 1000), y = 5e6 + runif(n, 0, 1000))
D  <- as.matrix(dist(xy))
field <- as.numeric(t(chol(exp(-D / 70) + diag(1e-8, n))) %*% rnorm(n))
xy$a  <- rnorm(n)
xy$b  <- rnorm(n)
xy$z  <- 1.5 * xy$a + field + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)
pts   <- st_as_sf(xy, coords = c("x", "y"), crs = 32632)
lm_fit <- function(train_sf, response_var = "z", predictor_vars = c("a", "b")) {
  d   <- st_drop_geometry(train_sf)
  # With no predictors the model is intercept-only: "z ~ 1", not "z ~ ".
  rhs <- if (length(predictor_vars)) paste(predictor_vars, collapse = " + ") else "1"
  fml <- as.formula(paste(response_var, "~", rhs))
  new_spatial_fit(
    subclass       = "lmsurf_fit",
    engine         = lm(fml, data = d),
    formula        = fml,
    response_var   = response_var,
    predictor_vars = predictor_vars,
    data_sf        = train_sf
  )
}
predict.lmsurf_fit <- function(object, newdata = NULL, ...) {
  if (is.null(newdata)) return(fitted(object$engine))
  as.numeric(predict(object$engine, newdata = st_drop_geometry(newdata)))
}
residuals.lmsurf_fit <- function(object, ...) residuals(object$engine)
fitted.lmsurf_fit    <- function(object, ...) fitted(object$engine)
for (g in c("predict", "residuals", "fitted"))
  registerS3method(g, "lmsurf_fit", get(paste0(g, ".lmsurf_fit")))

fit <- lm_fit(pts)

1. Structure left in the residuals 

mi <- residual_morans_i(fit)
mi
## Residual Moran's I = 0.4480   (E[I] = -0.0029, sd = 0.0253)
##   z = 17.841, p = 3.38e-71
##   null: residual moments, exact for these residuals; n = 350, df = 347, design rank 3
##   residual kurtosis 3.152 (3 = Gaussian)
##   weights: 350 x 350 dgCMatrix, 8 neighbour(s) per row; not retained, keep_weights = TRUE to keep it

A large positive Moran’s I says nearby residuals resemble each other, so the model is missing something that varies smoothly across the map. Here that is the simulated field, by construction.

Three parts of the print earn attention. The null says which moments the p-value came from: residual moments condition on the design matrix and are exact for OLS residuals, randomisation moments treat the residuals as exchangeable and are an approximation for any model. null = "auto" chooses per fit, so read what it chose. The design rank is the rank of the rebuilt model matrix, which is where the residual degrees of freedom come from. The kurtosis says how far the residuals sit from the Gaussian case the moments assume, with 3 as the reference.

The weight matrix is n×nn \times n and is described instead of returned. Ask for it when you want to reuse the same neighbours:

mi_w <- residual_morans_i(fit, keep_weights = TRUE)
dim(mi_w$weights)
## [1] 350 350
mi$weights_summary[c("n", "storage", "neighbours", "kept")]
## $n
## [1] 350
## 
## $storage
## [1] "dgCMatrix"
## 
## $neighbours
## [1] 8 8
## 
## $kept
## [1] FALSE

weights_summary is present either way, so a NULL in weights is always explained.

2. Standard errors on aggregated values

Aggregate the points into cells and the naive standard error of each cell mean is s/ns/\sqrt{n}, which treats the points in a cell as independent. For the cell’s own mean that is the right standard error when the points are spread through the cell. For the cell mean as an estimate of the population (grand) mean it is not: on an autocorrelated field the points in a cell share the cell’s departure from that mean, and the effective sample size is smaller than the count.

hull <- clip_target_for(pts, expand = 0.02, quiet = TRUE)
tess <- build_tessellation(pts, boundary = hull, method = "square",
                           approx_n_cells = 24, quiet = TRUE)
asg  <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, tess$cells)

c(cells = nrow(tess$cells), points = nrow(asg),
  median_per_cell = median(table(asg$poly_id)))
##           cells          points median_per_cell 
##              25             350              14

summarize_by_cell() takes a design effect, and three settings are worth comparing on the same cells.

sac  <- estimate_sac_range(pts, "z")
iid  <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", cells_sf = tess$cells, deff = 1)
kish <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", cells_sf = tess$cells, deff = "kish")
vgm  <- summarize_by_cell(asg, "z", cells_sf = tess$cells, deff = "variogram",
                          sac = sac)

data.frame(n         = iid$n,
           iid       = round(iid$..se_resp_z, 3),
           kish      = round(kish$..se_resp_z, 3),
           variogram = round(vgm$..se_resp_z, 3))[1:5, ]
##    n   iid  kish variogram
## 1 14 0.546 1.072     1.272
## 2 11 0.447 0.805     0.963
## 3 18 0.381 0.822     0.987
## 4 16 0.592 1.222     1.467
## 5  8 0.527 0.854     0.996

The median cell’s standard error is 1.96 times wider under kish and 2.35 times wider under variogram than the independent-sampling one. As an estimate of the population mean, a confidence interval built on the naive number is about half the width it should be on this field. For the cell’s own mean the naive standard error is the right one, and section 3 (kriging_adequacy()) covers that quantity.

deff = "kish" estimates an intra-class correlation from the within-cell and between-cell variance and applies Kish’s factor. deff = "variogram" takes the correlation from the fitted variogram model, so it uses the spatial structure rather than the cell labels. When no usable variogram exists that request falls back to "kish" with a warning, and the deff_method column names the correction each row carries. The choice is recorded:

str(attr(vgm, "deff_applied"))
## List of 6
##  $ method   : chr "variogram"
##  $ deff     : num [1:25] 4.12 3.49 5.11 4.65 2.71 ...
##  $ deff_rows: num [1:25] 4.12 3.49 5.11 4.65 2.71 ...
##  $ rbar     : num [1:25] 0.24 0.249 0.242 0.243 0.244 ...
##  $ crs      :List of 2
##   ..$ input: chr "EPSG:32632"
##   ..$ wkt  : chr "PROJCRS[\"WGS 84 / UTM zone 32N\",\n    BASEGEOGCRS[\"WGS 84\",\n        ENSEMBLE[\"World Geodetic System 1984 "| __truncated__
##   ..- attr(*, "class")= chr "crs"
##  $ max_n    : int 500
attr(kish, "icc")$resp
## [1] 0.1692353

A cell whose design effect reaches its point count carries no information about the variance at all, and its standard error is NA. That is a statement about the cell, so the fix is bigger cells or more points, not a different setting.

3. Is the cell mean the best estimate of the cell?

The plain mean weights every point in a cell equally and ignores everything outside it. Block kriging uses the fitted variogram, borrows from neighbouring cells, and reports a variance derived from the spatial model. kriging_adequacy() runs both and compares them.

ka <- kriging_adequacy(asg, "z", tess$cells, k = 4, seed = 1)
ka
## Block-kriging adequacy over 25 cells (350 points, nmax 50)
##   variogram: Nug(2.34, 0) + Exp(1.49, 208); sill 3.83, nugget 2.34 (61%), range 623.8
##   kriging variance / no-data variance of the cell mean (1 = nothing from the data): median 0.130, range 0.090-0.217; 0 cell(s) above 0.5
##   kr_gain, the share of the plain mean's error variance that kriging removes under this variogram (1 - kr_var / plain_var): median 0.44, range 0.23-0.59 over the 25 cell(s) with points and a kriged estimate
##   kriged minus plain mean, over the standard deviation the variogram gives that difference (sqrt(plain_var - kr_var)): |shift| > 1 in 7 of 25 cell(s), > 2 in 0 (about 8 and 1 when the variogram is right)
##   naive s^2/n below plain_var (the naive standard error is too small if the variogram is right) in 15 of the 25 cell(s) with two or more points; median s^2/n over plain_var 0.85
##   empty cells: 0 (kriged estimate and variance available for each)
##   blocked CV (block_kfold, 4 folds, 350 points): var of standardised error 0.96 (1 = kriging variance correct; above 1 = understated), mean -0.04, RMSE 1.76

Four readings. plain_var is the error variance of the plain mean under the fitted variogram; a naive se^2 below it says the naive standard error was optimistic. kr_gain is the share of that variance kriging removes in the cell. kr_shift is how far the kriged estimate moved from the plain mean, over the standard deviation the variogram gives that difference: about a third of cells beyond 1 and one in twenty beyond 2 is what a right variogram produces, and more says the means and the model disagree. The blocked cross-validation at the end standardises each held-out error by its kriging variance: a variance of 1 means the kriging variance is right, and above 1 means it is understated.

head(st_drop_geometry(ka)[, c("n", "mean", "se", "plain_var", "kr_pred", "kr_var",
                             "kr_gain", "kr_shift")], 4)
## Block-kriging adequacy (subset; the fitted summary is not carried by a subset)
##    n      mean        se plain_var   kr_pred    kr_var   kr_gain   kr_shift
## 1 14 1.1020196 0.5463243 0.2142987 0.9482129 0.1388290 0.3521708 -0.5598719
## 2 11 0.3804887 0.4470487 0.3160037 0.5214518 0.1528265 0.5163774  0.3489599
## 3 18 1.0791003 0.3805235 0.1817638 0.8801141 0.1183908 0.3486557 -0.7904436
## 4 16 1.5055114 0.5920044 0.1846308 1.2414270 0.1078652 0.4157788 -0.9531463

An empty cell still gets a kriged estimate and variance, which is the practical reason to run this: a tessellation fine enough to be useful usually has cells with no observation in them. This grid has none, as the report’s empty cells line says, because 25 cells over 350 points leaves every cell populated; the reporting vignette’s grid over the North Carolina counties has five.

4. Where the score applies

A cross-validated number describes the region the training data covers. For predictions made anywhere else, it describes nothing. area_of_applicability() marks the difference, following Meyer and Pebesma (2021).

grid <- create_grid_polygons(hull, target_cells = 200, type = "square")
gp   <- suppressWarnings(st_centroid(grid))
set.seed(2)
gp$a <- rnorm(nrow(gp))
gp$b <- rnorm(nrow(gp), mean = 3)     # shifted well outside the training range

aoa <- area_of_applicability(gp, model = fit)
aoa
## Area of applicability (Meyer & Pebesma 2021)
## 
##   predictors  : 2 (a, b)
##   weighted    : no (all predictors count equally: the model carries no variable importance)
##   training    : 350 points
##   reference   : nearest other training point (no folds supplied)
##   normaliser  : 1.7610 (mean pairwise distance)
##   threshold   : 0.1552 (outlier-removed max of training DI)
##   location    : not measured
## 
##   64 of 225 prediction points inside the AOA (28.4%)
## 
## Predictions outside the AOA are extrapolations; the cross-validated
## performance estimate does not cover them.
plot(aoa)

Shifting one predictor three standard deviations moves most of the grid outside the domain the model was trained on. The dissimilarity index DI is on aoa$aoa, alongside the logical AOA, and threshold is the cutoff derived from the training data.

One trap worth stating plainly. AOA is NA wherever a predictor was missing or non-finite, !NA is NA, and R skips NA positions in a subscripted assignment. Test for TRUE:

inside <- !is.na(aoa$aoa$AOA) & aoa$aoa$AOA
c(inside = sum(inside), outside_or_unknown = sum(!inside))
##             inside outside_or_unknown 
##                 64                161

5. Two ways to leak

Coordinates as predictors. A model given x and y can reproduce the training surface by memorising location, and random folds will not detect it. fit_rf_model(include_coords = TRUE) logs a caution (once per session) for this reason. Score any such model with blocked folds, and read vignette("spatial-cross-validation") for what the blocking has to be wide enough to do.

Selection outside the fold. Choosing predictors on the whole data set and then cross-validating the chosen set gives the selection a look at every test row. select_features_forward() does the selection inside the resampling, and it takes the fold scheme as an argument for the same reason the outer loop does. Blocked folds only keep test rows apart from training rows if the blocks are at least as wide as the autocorrelation range. make_folds() estimates that range for what the candidates leave unexplained, about 320 m on this field, and warns when the blocks are narrower. The default grid here has blocks about 250 m across, so block_size = 400 is passed:

# select_features_forward() calls fit_fn(train_sf, vars), so the learner above
# needs an adapter that puts `vars` in the predictor slot. Step 0 fits it with
# no predictors at all, which is why lm_fit() builds "z ~ 1" for an empty set.
sel_fn <- function(train_sf, vars) lm_fit(train_sf, "z", vars)

sel <- select_features_forward(pts, "z", c("a", "b"), fit_fn = sel_fn,
                               k = 4, method = "block_kfold",
                               block_size = 400, seed = 1)
sel$selected
## [1] "a"
sel$history
##   step variable    score n_pred         gain    fold_gain fold_gain_se
## 1    0   <none> 1.886912    350           NA           NA           NA
## 2    1        a 1.113470    350  0.773441581  0.758268480 0.0635599357
## 3    1        b 1.887999    350 -0.001087626 -0.001111525 0.0003395323
## 4    2        b 1.116468    350 -0.002998125 -0.002133347 0.0038235429

history has one row per candidate scored at each step. Step 0 is the intercept-only model, so a had to beat it to be added, and at step 2 adding the noise variable b made the cross-validated RMSE slightly worse, so the selection stopped at a. A candidate is added when its pooled gain exceeds tol and the mean of its per-fold gains (fold_gain) exceeds one standard error of that mean (fold_gain_se), from step 1 on; rule = "tol" tests the pooled gain alone.

Its inner folds default to the scheme you pass. Passing random_kfold there logs a caution, because a leaky inner loop can select a variable for being spatially close to the response and an honest outer loop will then report a respectable number for a dishonestly chosen feature set.

6. Warnings about pooled cell values

summarize_by_cell() returns by default, beside each cell’s mean, a pooled value: the mean pulled toward the mean of the cells around it. What it has to say about those values, and about whether the cells are the ones their count was chosen for, comes as R warnings with a class. Each is raised once per call and reason and carries its numbers as fields, so it can be caught and read without matching its text; a warning about the pooled columns also names the columns it applies to. This vignette hides warnings, so the helper below runs a call and returns the classes it raised:

raised <- function(expr) {
  seen <- character(0)
  withCallingHandlers(expr, warning = function(w) {
    seen <<- c(seen, class(w)[1])
    invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
  })
  seen
}

The cells are built for pooled values at 4.5 observations per cell, by the calls vignette("resolution") and vignette("reporting") walk through. Those are the defaults, so nothing is named but the response; estimate = "mean" in the summary gives the plain means alone, and vignette("resolution") lists the profile’s earlier defaults:

prof  <- resolution_profile(pts, "z")
size  <- select_resolution(prof)
seeds <- get_voronoi_seeds(method = "kmeans", n = size, sample_points = pts)
vor   <- build_tessellation(seeds, method = "voronoi", quiet = TRUE)
asg_v <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, vor$cells, polygon_id_col = "cell_id")

raised(summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = vor$cells))
## character(0)

A summary of the cell value the count was chosen for, on the cells and rows that were scored, raises nothing. Each of the five warnings below is a departure from that.

spatialkit_estimate_mismatch: the count was chosen for the other cell value. The selection wrote down that the count was set for pooled values, the cells and the assigned layer carried that record, and this call asks for plain means:

w <- tryCatch(
  summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "z", id_col = "cell_id", cells_sf = vor$cells,
                    estimate = "mean"),
  spatialkit_estimate_mismatch = function(w) w)
unlist(unclass(w)[c("chosen_for", "reported", "rule", "cells")])
## chosen_for   reported       rule      cells 
##   "pooled"     "mean"     "size"       "78"

The summary is returned as asked. Report the value the count was chosen for, or choose the count for the value reported: resolution_profile(estimate = "mean") with select_resolution(criterion = "loo").

spatialkit_cells_differ: these are not the cells and rows that were scored. The summary fits the response again on what it is given and compares the rows, the cells that hold one and the leave-one-out error with the record. Here twenty rows were dropped after the assignment:

w <- tryCatch(
  summarize_by_cell(asg_v[-(1:20), ], "z", id_col = "cell_id",
                    cells_sf = vor$cells),
  spatialkit_cells_differ = function(w) w)
w$what
## [1] "n"
rbind(scored = unlist(w$scored), found = unlist(w$found))
##          n cells      loo
## scored 350    78 2.935117
## found  330    78 3.004029

what names the first comparison that failed: "n" for another number of rows with a response, "cells" for another number of cells that hold one, "loo" for the same rows in the same number of cells with another error, which means rows sit in other cells, and "record" when the assigned layer and cells_sf carry different records. The usual causes are rows filtered after the assignment, a boundary that leaves points in no cell, and a layer other than the one profiled. On gridded locations a row can lie the same distance from two centres, on the boundary between their cells. The profile scores it in the cell of the lower-numbered centre, and assign_features_to_polygons() gives a point there the same cell when the cells carry the record of the centres scored, so a lattice passes the check. build_tessellation() draws those cells in the profile’s CRS whatever CRS the seeds come back in. Cells built in another projected CRS, named with its crs, are the nearest-centre cells of that CRS, so rows near a boundary, on it or not, can sit in another cell, and the warning then speaks of them. The values returned describe the cells as given, and attr(, "count_rule")$check keeps the outcome. Cells the caller brings carry no record and are not checked.

spatialkit_no_structure: the cells predict no better than one mean. b is noise by construction:

noise <- summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "b", id_col = "cell_id")
raised(summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "b", id_col = "cell_id"))
## [1] "spatialkit_no_structure"
as.data.frame(attr(noise, "pooled")$columns$resp_b[
  c("loo", "loo_one_cell", "structure_p", "own_weight", "structured")])
##        loo loo_one_cell structure_p own_weight structured
## 1 1.109034     1.074528   0.7556459 0.03572578      FALSE

structured is FALSE when the leave-one-out error of one mean for all rows (loo_one_cell) is within 2 percent of that of the pooled values (loo) or below it, or when the F test of the cell means against one mean has p >= 0.05. The values are returned, and a map of them still looks smooth, because each is mostly the mean of its neighbours. On 200 simulated layers with white noise as the response the median own weight was 0.11 and a cell’s pooled value had a correlation of 0.79 with the mean of its 8 nearest cells’ values, where the plain means had one of -0.02 (dev/sim-pooled-values.R in the package’s repository; ?summarize_by_cell gives the settings). Read the warning as: one mean describes this column, and the map shows the pooling.

spatialkit_pool_degenerate: the values were computed and carry no pooling. Its reason says which of three cases it is. A column that does not vary inside any cell is one of them:

asg_v$flat <- 1
w <- tryCatch(summarize_by_cell(asg_v, "flat", id_col = "cell_id"),
              spatialkit_pool_degenerate = function(w) w)
w$reason
## [1] "no spread inside any cell"

With "no spread inside any cell" and with "one cell" every own weight is 1 and the pooled value is the plain mean. With "no signal between cells" the cell means differ from their neighbours’ by no more than the spread inside the cells explains: every own weight is 0, and each pooled value is the mean of the cell’s neighbours and holds none of the cell’s own observations. That last case is not the test for a response without structure. In the simulation it came on 20 of the 200 white-noise layers and spatialkit_no_structure on all 200.

spatialkit_pool_few_cells: 2 to 9 cells. The neighbours of a cell are then all the other cells, so its target is the mean of every observation outside it:

few   <- create_grid_polygons(hull, target_cells = 4, type = "square")
asg_f <- assign_features_to_polygons(pts, few, quiet = TRUE)
raised(four <- summarize_by_cell(asg_f, "z"))
## [1] "spatialkit_pool_few_cells"
as.data.frame(four)[, c("poly_id", "n", "resp_mean_z", "..pooled_resp_z",
                        "..pooled_w_resp_z", "..pooled_target_resp_z")]
##   poly_id  n resp_mean_z ..pooled_resp_z ..pooled_w_resp_z
## 1       1 88  0.06747028     0.085370087         0.8870278
## 2       2 90  0.89167351     0.786488402         0.8892603
## 3       4 96 -0.18343249    -0.130203153         0.8954580
## 4       5 76 -0.04541381    -0.007411179         0.8714826
##   ..pooled_target_resp_z
## 1             0.22591468
## 2            -0.05816763
## 3             0.32573445
## 4             0.25028643

The overall mean lies between a cell’s own mean and that target. A cell whose own weight is below its share of the observations therefore gets a pooled value on the far side of the overall mean from its plain mean, and two cells can change order. The ..pooled_w_* column shows how close each cell is to that, and estimate = "mean" gives the plain means.

?summarize_by_cell lists these classes and the others of the pooled values under “Conditions”, with the fields each carries.

Next

vignette("spatial-cross-validation") covers fold schemes and block sizing. vignette("resolution") covers choosing the cell count these diagnostics are computed over. ?residual_morans_i documents the two nulls and when each is exact, ?summarize_by_cell derives the design-effect correction and reports its measured coverage, and ?area_of_applicability covers the weighting and the threshold.
